10702-the-history-of-rome-book-ii-from-t:
Theodor Mommsen, the German historian whose History of Rome won lasting fame, traces Book II from the fall of Rome's kings to the union of Italy. William Purdie Dickson's translation, made with Mommsen's sanction and revised throughout, carries the story through the early republic: its wars, laws, and the slow binding of Italian peoples under Roman rule.

Mommsen combines legal insight with narrative drive, explaining how Rome's institutions grew from conflict and compromise. The book is dense but rewarding, and it shaped how later historians understood Rome. Readers meet the republic taking shape, in a classic work of nineteenth-century scholarship.
13500-a-heroine-of-france-the-story-of-j:
Evelyn Everett-Green tells Joan of Arc's story through a narrator who first hears of the Maid, then sees her, and follows her to Vaucouleurs, Chinon, and the king. Chapters trace trial and testing, the march for Orleans, command at Orleans, battle, triumph, trouble, and the raising of the siege.

A man who falls from a castle passage into a swollen stream is called by some a victim of witchcraft, by most a sign that the Maid could read the future. Dunois and La Hire, led from confidence in Joan to listen to detractors, anger the narrator, who still boils at the thought. Everett-Green writes a girl's heroine tale of faith, war, and a young commander.
16933-joan-of-arc:
Lord Ronald Gower, trustee of the National Portrait Gallery, wrote this 1893 life of Joan of Arc, issued by John C. Nimmo in London with ten pictures, seven etchings and three photo-etchings. Gower dedicates it to his mother's memory. He notes her cult for the heroine and the bronze statue she placed at Cliveden. That statue bears words on the great pity in the kingdom of France. A picture of Tour Coudray at Chinon fronts the book.

Gower tells Joan's life from village maid to warrior and martyr, with admiration for all that is good, beautiful, and high-minded in her. His tone is Victorian and reverent. The book gives a handsome, illustrated life of the Maid of Orleans, useful for readers who want a 1800s view of Joan before modern scholarship reshaped her story.
26329-the-inquisition-a-critical-and-his:
E. Vacandard's Inquisition, translated by Bertrand L. Conway and issued in a new edition in 1915, studies the coercive power of the Church with Catholic scholarly care. It opens by weighing Henry Charles Lea's three-volume History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, published in 1888 and praised as the most thorough history yet. Vacandard grants its range but denies it the last word.

Later pages trace how old Roman law sent Manicheans to the stake, how Gregory IX took a stern line in 1231, and how the Council of Toulouse in 1229 ordered heretics condemned. The book carries a Nihil Obstat and the imprimatur of Archbishop Farley. It offers a critical, documented counterpoint to Lea, from inside the Church's own tradition.
26357-is-the-young-man-absalom-safe-a-se:
David Wright, vicar of St. Mary Magdalene, Stoke Bishop, preached this sermon on Sunday, July 19, 1885. His text is 2 Samuel 18:29, King David's anxious question about his rebel son Absalom: is the young man safe? Wright uses the verse to ask whether the young men of his own day are safe in character and faith.

He argues that Bible figures feel real because their faults are shown plainly, unlike heroes shaped by a historian's favor. Then he turns to his hearers, warning that a nation sinks when its youth lose energy, gentleness, kindness, manliness, and purity. The sermon closes by urging each young listener to hold fast to faith in the living God.
31734-extract-from-a-sermon-delivered-at:
The Reverend F. T. Gray's Tribute to a Good Man is an extract from a sermon delivered at the Bulfinch Street Church, Boston, on January 9, 1853. It came the Sunday following the interment of the late Amos Lawrence. John Wilson and Son published it at Boston in 1853, and the pages are respectfully dedicated to Lawrence's memory. Gray's sermon honors a merchant and philanthropist of Boston at his burial week.

The extract preserves the pulpit's farewell to a good man, praising a life of usefulness and charity. It is a short memorial piece, and it shows how a congregation marked the passing of one of its leading citizens.
31965-the-cathedrals-of-northern-spain-t:
Charles Rudy's Cathedrals of Northern Spain, in L. C. Page and Company's Cathedral Series alongside Francis Miltoun's volumes on France and the Rhine, covers Galicia, the north, and western and eastern Castile. Its contents run from Santiago de Compostela, Corunna, Mondoñedo, Lugo, Orense, Tuy, Bayona, and Vigo through Oviedo, Leon, Burgos, and Santander to Salamanca, Toledo, and Segovia.

Part one offers introductory studies in general remarks and historical and architectural arabesques, before the regional chapters describe each cathedral in turn, with an appendix and index. Readers get a richly illustrated architectural guide to Spain's northern cathedrals, for travelers who love church-building.
32251-applied-physiology-including-the-e:
Frank Overton's Applied Physiology, including the effects of alcohol and narcotics, was published by the American Book Company in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. Its copyrights date from 1898 and 1910. Overton, late house surgeon to the City Hospital in New York, wrote it for the primary grade. Its chapters are short, plain, and schoolroom-ready. Its contents run from Cells and Of What Cells Are Made through digestion in mouth and stomach to Foods.

Later chapters treat Tobacco, Fermentation, and Kinds of Strong Drink. They continue through Blood, Breathing, Heat, and Clothing, the Skin and Kidneys, the Nerves, Spinal Cord, and Brain, the Senses, and Bones and Joints. Readers get a primary-school physiology text with a temperance purpose: the body's workings explained alongside the harms of drink and drugs, in language a young pupil can follow.
37706-john-ronge-the-holy-coat-of-treves:
John Ronge and the Holy Coat of Treves is a pamphlet on the new German-Catholic Church, printed at Edinburgh in 1845 for Nelson. A warning from Luther, aimed at this very coat in 1814, heads the title page. Luther asks how the devil dressed up dead bones, garments, and vessels into holy ones, and how confidently people believed the liars and crowded on pilgrimages.

The pamphlet opens its case by quoting the authorized account published at Treves itself. Thirty-four years before, the tract recalls, the city held 200,000 strangers longing after the holy relic. Between twenty and thirty thousand pilgrims were quartered in the city nightly, and the order and devotion of the ceremony lived in memory. Ronge, a priest who protested the 1844 exhibition of the coat, became the pamphlet's hero: his stand sparked a breakaway church in Germany.
39590-some-account-of-llangollen-and-its:
Simpson wrote this account of Llangollen and its vicinity, with a circuit of about seven miles, published in London in 1827. He dedicated it, by permission, to Lady Eleanor Butler and Miss Ponsonby, the famous Ladies of Llangollen at Plas Newydd. Chance had made him a resident of the town, and the advertisement says its beauty moved him to collect its history.

The contents map the small tour in full. The town and its church come first, then Offa's Dyke, Chirk Castle, and Brynkinallt. The Berwyn Mountains, the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct, and Castell Dinas Bran follow. The river Dee, the vale of Glyn Dyfrdwy, and the Pillar of Eliseg close the round. Simpson writes for visitors who would walk the ground with a book in hand. Readers get a Welsh border town as its own neighbors prized it, in the age of the picturesque tour.
43461-ninth-annual-report-of-the-st-mary:
The Ninth Annual Report of the St Mary Abbott, Kensington, District Visiting Society was transcribed from the eighteen fifty three W Birch edition. The report gives some account of the societies subordinate or affiliated to it. Archdeacon Sinclair, the vicar, served as president. Sir J Conroy and Sir Henry Willock were vice presidents. Mr Clarke was treasurer, and the curates joint secretaries.

A committee list names Mr Bailey, Dr Bayford, Rev J H Howlett, and others of the parish. Alfred Ellis of Lower Phillimore Place was collector. Ladies or gentlemen desirous of taking charge of districts as visitors are asked to write the secretaries, the notice says. The secretaries will give all information in their power to any subscriber, it adds. Parish accounts, visitor reports, and society news fill the pamphlet. Local historians get Victorian parish charity in full working order.
45743-joan-of-arc:
Joan of Arc is a biography by Laura Richards, published by Appleton of New York and London in 1919. Richards had written lives of Florence Nightingale, Abigail Adams, and Elizabeth Fry. She dedicates the book to the memory of Theodore Roosevelt, also a soldier.

Sixteen chapters follow Joan from Domrémy to Rouen. Chapter titles mark the road: The Voices, The Empty Throne, Vaucouleurs and Chinon, and Recognition. Then come Orleans, The Relief, The Deliverance, and The Week of Victories. Rheims, Paris, and Compiègne lead to the chapter at Rouen. The book opens with a poem by Theodosia Garrison, The Soul of Jeanne d'Arc. In it Joan stands not as a dumb saint but as a straight young soldier, confident and strong.
45846-letters-exhibiting-the-most-promin:
Orson Spencer, president of the Latter Day Saints church in Europe, published letters at Liverpool in 1848 in reply to the Reverend William Crowell of Boston. A motto from Daniel heads the title: the wise shall understand. Contents list Crowell's letter first. Spencer's replies treat general remarks, then immediate revelation. Faith and water baptism follow.

The gift of the Holy Ghost and apostasy from the primitive church come next. The re establishment of an apostolic church closes the visible list. Spencer was a Baptist trained scholar turned Mormon missionary. His letters became a standard Mormon doctrinal work. Liverpool was the church's British publishing hub.
48470-the-story-of-joan-of-arc:
Andrew Lang wrote The Story of Joan of Arc for young readers who love the Maid. J Jellicoe drew the pictures for the book of nineteen hundred six. Lang gave it to Angela Cottrell-Dormer, a young friend of Joan. His gift letter dares scoffers to read the trial first.

Five great books by Quicherat hold her trial in full, he says. Friends and foes who knew her swore to each fact there. Joan was born at Domremy on January sixth, fourteen hundred twelve. She could not read, write, or ride when her call came. Yet she led French hosts at not quite seventeen years old. Wounds could not stop her from the front of her men. At nineteen she was burned, her foes finding no true charge. Her wish in glory was her father’s cot and her mother’s side.
48514-the-lake-dwellings-of-europe-being:
Robert Munro, secretary of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, lectured on the lake dwellings of Europe as the Rhind Lectures in Archaeology for 1888. The lectures were printed in London in 1890. Munro had written on ancient Scottish lake dwellings or crannogs. The society left him no choice of subject, he says, and the proposal came as a complete surprise.

Munro pondered the task with considerable misgiving, since his special knowledge then ran to Scotland alone. Relics from the great settlements lay scattered widely, and forming a clear notion of their civilization took hard labour. His lectures survey pile villages on lakes from Switzerland outward, their tools, food, and craft, in a founding work of the field.
51049-modern-french-prisons-bice-tre-st-:
Major Arthur Griffiths wrote on modern French prisons for a set on crime. The Grolier Society issued the work in London in a run of one thousand sets. Griffiths had served as an inspector of prisons in Great Britain. The copy shown is Number 307 of the National form.

Bicetre, Sainte Pelagie, Saint Lazare, La Force, and the Conciergerie lead the survey. A front plate shows Madame Roland in Sainte Pelagie, from a painting by E Carpentier. Chapters treat famed convicts, the first great detective, and model reform schools. Readers gain a full, grim tour of French cells and their reform.
52714-sermons-on-the-scriptural-principl:
Edward Hoare, curate of Richmond in Surrey, preached these sermons, printed by J Hatchard and Son of London in 1845. Parishioners asked him to print them, and he owns both a deep sense of their flaws and a firm faith in their truth. The sermons set out the scriptural grounds of the Protestant church.

Hoare had also written tracts against transubstantiation and the invocation of saints, sold cheap by the hundred. The matter here turns on Rome: he holds that its decrees, if changed, break its claim never to err, and if kept, stand as old errors. Eternal truth changes not, he argues, so whoever changes must have been wrong before or after. The sermons plead the case in pulpit form.
52887-eclectic-magazine-of-foreign-liter:
The March 1885 number of the Eclectic Magazine of Foreign Literature, Science, and Art reprints the best pieces from British and foreign periodicals for American readers. The issue is volume forty-one, number three of the new series, the old series having run to sixty-three volumes.

The lead article is From Siberia to Switzerland, the story of an escape, by William Westall. Westall explains why escapes from Eastern Siberia so seldom succeed. The distances are immense, the climate terrible, money lacking, and the fugitive must keep to the high roads. Even in Germany a runaway may be seized again, so true safety lies only in England, France, or Switzerland. Westall calls the life of a political exile in the far east or north horrible beyond telling, and his tale shows what a rare joining of lucky chances a full escape demands.
56277-derelicts-an-account-of-ships-lost:
Derelicts is an account of ships lost at sea in general commercial traffic, with a brief history of blockade runners stranded along the North Carolina coast from 1861 to 1865. James Sprunt of Wilmington wrote it, and it was printed in 1920. A frontispiece shows the chase of the Lilian. Sprunt also wrote Chronicles of the Cape Fear River.

In his foreword Sprunt tells that about twenty-five years earlier he wrote a series of stories of the Cape Fear blockade for the Southport Leader. They came from his personal experiences as a participant in the blockade runners Advance, Eugenie, North Heath, Lilian, and Susan Beirne, and finally in the Alonzo. The stories greatly interested the Cape Fear pilots who had taken part with him in that hazardous service. The book is dedicated to a professor of history at the University of North Carolina.
58364-the-wreck-of-the-royal-charter-com:
Frank Fowler, late of Her Majesty's Civil Service in New South Wales, compiled The Wreck of the Royal Charter from authentic sources with some original matter, published at London in 1859. Contents hold an introductory note, the narrative of the wreck, and the press on the catastrophe.

A list of steerage passengers, Dr Scoresby on the ship, the adjourned inquest, its verdict, and latest details from Molfra follow. The note confesses the book was prepared in haste to save the mail leaving England on the twelfth, yet aims to be a complete narrative. The Royal Charter, homeward bound from Australia with gold, broke up off Anglesey in the great storm of October 1859. Readers get the disaster written while the wreckage was still news.
64249-holmes-own-story-in-which-the-alle:
Holmes' Own Story is the prison written account of H W Mudgett, known as Holmes. It was entered for copyright in eighteen ninety five at Washington. Its subtitle calls him an alleged multi murderer and arch conspirator. Twenty two tragic deaths and disappearances are named in its promise. A prison diary from Moyamensing forms an appendix.

In his preface Holmes says the pages were written in prison while he awaited trial. He wrote against the advice of friends and the direct orders of his counsel, he owns. For months the press has vilified him, he complains. He has been held up as the most atrocious criminal of the age, he writes. The book promises a full narrative of his life. His dealings with a man named Pitezel and that man's children fill much of it.
64896-the-men-of-the-merchant-service-be:
The Men of the Merchant Service, being the polity of the mercantile marine for longshore readers, by Frank Bullen, was published in London in 1900 by Smith, Elder. Bullen wrote The Cruise of the Cachalot and The Log of a Sea-Waif. The book is dedicated to Rudyard Kipling, in grateful recognition of his genius and his kindness to the author.

The preface states the gap Bullen means to fill. Among all the works of fact and fiction on the sea, he says, none tells in a full way what conditions of life in the merchant service really are. A parent whose son begs to go to sea has nowhere to turn for the whole picture in one handy volume. Bullen, who shipped before the mast himself, supplies it: officers, men, food, discipline, and the law of the ship.
a-heroine-of-france-the-story-of-joan-of: Evelyn Everett Green tells the story of Joan of Arc, heroine of France. Chapters follow how the narrator first heard of the Maid, first saw her, and watched her come to Vaucouleurs. Joan is tried and tested, journeys to Chinon, and marches for Orleans. Green tells the Maid's triumphs and troubles for young readers.
britannica-1911-buffon-george-louis-lecl:
Buffon, George Louis Leclerc, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French naturalist. Born on the 7th of September 1707 at Montbard, he was a law man's son. He read law at a Jesuit college in Dijon as a youth. But a strong bent for science and maths showed in him early.

He toured Italy and England with a young English lord named Kingston. In 1735 he brought out a French version of a work by Hales. Five years later he did the same for a work of Newton. At age twenty-five he came into a large sum from his mother. From then his life went to steady work in science. In 1739 he took charge of the King's Garden and Museum.
britannica-1911-joan-of-arc:
Joan of Arc, called Jeanne d'Arc in France, lived from about 1411 to 1431. The 1911 Britannica life hails her as the Maid of Orleans in war. She was born at Domremy, a small village in the Vosges hills. Her father Jacques Darc was a peasant who held his own land. Her mother Isabeau came from the village of Vouthon near by.

Her parents lived in easy means, yet Joan never learned to read. She could not write either, the entry notes with pointed care. Her mother taught her the Pater Noster, Ave Maria, and Credo by heart. At times she watched her father's flocks in the fields at home. At her trial in 1431 she scorned the name of shepherd girl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joan-of-ar:
Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orléans, carried a peasant girl's voices to a king's coronation and a martyr's fire. Born at Domremy in Champagne, probably on 6 January 1412, she was youngest of five children of Jacques d'Arc. Her father was a small farmer, poor but not needy. She never learned to read or write, but sewed and spun skilfully. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates her death at Rouen to 30 May 1431.

Domremy stayed loyal to Charles VII while Burgundians allied with England. Rehabilitation witnesses called Joan singularly pious, grave beyond years, often kneeling absorbed in church prayer, loving the poor tenderly. The popular image of a shepherdess childhood is, the entry says, quite unfounded. When Orléans was besieged from October 1428, her voices grew urgent, even threatening. She yielded, entered Orléans on 30 April 1429, and by 8 May English forts fell. Reims crowning followed that summer.
doe-osti-2574822-real-time-neutron-multi:
Report LA-UR-25-27654, issued July 30, 2025, carries a doctoral research proposal by Natalie Lauren Cannon of Georgia Tech, written with Los Alamos committee members. The problem is criticality safety while crews remove fuel debris from a damaged reactor. Workers need to know, in real time, how much neutron multiplication is happening and where the neutron sources sit, in a scene that keeps changing as debris moves.

The proposed tool is NoMAD, a Neutron Multiplication Analysis Detector. One thread adapts multiplicity counting, the standard way to assay fissile material, to dynamic environments where static assumptions fail. A second thread reads spatial count patterns across the detector to localize sources, using machine learning such as random forest regression. The threads merge in a joint method. Test data come from the beryllium-reflected plutonium ball at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingMartinLuthe:
In June 1999, the Journal of American History ran a short book review, on page 314, of a work about the Poor People's Campaign. The campaign was the protest movement Martin Luther King Jr. was organizing when he was killed in 1968. The review looks at the book's account of King's final project and the forces working against it.

One thread the review takes up is the FBI's effort to discredit King. It also weighs a harder question: whether the campaign, under King's personal direction, might actually have reached its goals. Readers interested in King, the FBI, or the politics of 1968 will find the review a compact guide to that debate.
joan-of-arc:
Joan of Arc is a life of the Maid of Orleans by Lord Ronald Gower, a trustee of the National Portrait Gallery. The London book carries ten illustrations, seven etchings and three photo-etchings. Gower dedicates it to his mother, who held Joan in deep reverence, almost a cult. A bronze statue of Joan stood in her house at Cliveden.

On the statue's pedestal stood words Gower takes as summing up Joan's life. They speak of the great pity that there was in the kingdom of France. He wrote the book hoping his mother would have approved its feeling. His preface, dated from Arcachon on November 29, opens the life that follows. The portrait is admiring from the start, a short life of France's heroine for general readers.
podcast-tuckercarlson-S50ccZWljrc:
Tucker Carlson argues that dragging American troops deeper into war with Iran serves no clear gain. He says no one can state, in calm points, how the nation wins. Critics attack those who ask, he says, but offer no plan.

The title warns the war will cripple the United States. It also claims Israel's violence has a deeper goal. Carlson urges viewers to demand a real case before more troops go. The episode is a direct anti-war brief, built for listeners already doubtful about another long Middle East fight. His case rests on cost, risk, and past wars.
podcast-tuckercarlson-sDJmvLrWcRc:
Comedian Owen Benjamin joins Tucker Carlson to talk about his break with the Daily Wire and the dark side of Hollywood. The title also names conspiracy lore and comic Nick Fuentes. Benjamin was once a film actor who left that world.

Benjamin tells how his jokes and views cost him his place in the trade. He lays out his charge that Hollywood eats the young and guards its own. Carlson draws out his life since the fall, on a farm far from the lots. Listeners get a comic's raw tale of fame lost. The library keeps the talk as a record of his stated views.
the-history-of-rome-book-ii-from-the-abo: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome, Book II. The book covers the span from the end of the monarchy to the union of Italy. William Purdie Dickson translated it with the author's sanction. Dickson was a professor of divinity in Glasgow. The German original is named as Roemische Geschichte, Zweites Buch. Only the title page is present here. A preparer's note on marking foreign words also appears. The history itself does not appear.
